How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener's cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics. In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

[div-01]

The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):

Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening

In recent years, a significant amount of research within the neuroscience of music has been focused on the question of the relation between musicality and language (e.g., Patel, 2010; Peretz & Coltheart, 2003; Peretz, et al., 2015; 2018). Some researchers have argued for neurocognitive modularity between music and speech (e.g., Peretz & Coltheart, 2003; Perruchet & Poulin-Charronnat, 2013), while others have argued that music and speech share processing resources (e.g., Gordon et al., 2010; Mantell & Pfordresher, 2013; Schön et al., 2010 , Vuvan et al., 2015).

Yet others (e.g., Asano et al., 2021; Patel, 2003; Slevc & Okada, 2015) have attempted to integrate these views by theorizing different degrees of neurocognitive sharing for different levels of processing and by separating domain-specific representations (e.g., of music and speech) from processing mechanisms (e.g., syntax, cognitive control, executive function). Recent work provides interesting evidence for sharing at some levels of processing (e.g., neurons responding selectively to song in the auditory cortex; Norman-Haignere et al., 2022), and separation at other levels (e.g., dissociation between language and music processing in individually-defined language networks in the brain, Chen et al., 2023). Peretz et al. (2015; 2018) note that one of the major challenges for cognitive neuroscientists exploring language-music interactions is that "Cognitive demands made by supposedly analogous operations in processing music and speech may widely differ." Put differently, experiments that compare music in one condition and language in another may contain confounds due to differences in acoustics, stimulus complexity, or task difficulty between those conditions. As one example, Angulo-Perkins et al. (2014) found an area in the anterior superior temporal gyrus (aSTG) that responded more strongly to music than to speech. However, whether this effect emerged in the aSTG because of a categorical difference between music and speech versus uncontrolled acoustic differences between the music and speech clips is unclear.

One potential solution is to develop tasks based on stimuli such as the speechto-song illusion (Deutsch, Henthorn, & Lapidis, 2011), which participants are able to perceive as both speech and music (Peretz et al., 2015; 2018). Indeed, significant effort has gone to exploring this illusion by defining its acoustic and cognitive structure (Castro et al, 2018; Falk et al., 2014; Tierney et al., 2018), neurocognitive signatures (Tierney et al., 2013), individual differences governing its perception (Jaisin et al., 2016; Smit & Rathcke, 2024; Vanden Bosch der Nederlanden, et al., 2015) and contextual factors that impact the illusion (Margulis et al., 2015; Groenveld et al., 2019; Simchy-Gross & Margulis, 2018; Graber et al., 2017).

A novel approach for comparative study of language and music processing would be to model performance on a song perception task (which contains both speech and musical information) as a function of the strength of individual differences in listening style. Specifically, some listeners will be more focused on the lyrics (words, vocals, story) of the song, whereas others will be more focused on the musical aspects (pitch, rhythm, timbre). When processing songs, individuals high on lyric focus would be predicted to perform better on lyric tasks than pitch tasks, with the opposite pattern predicted for individuals who score low on lyric focus. Differences in brain activity that track this performance difference could then be used to refine the dynamics of brain networks subserving language and music processing. The study of lyric focus therefore creates a unique scientific opportunity for ongoing debates about language-music modularity.

Beyond advancing research on language and music, researchers interested in using songs as experimental stimuli would benefit from the measurement of lyric focus, as this individual difference could fundamentally change a participant's access to different aspects of the song signal. For instance, a researcher interested in emotions evoked during song listening might expect different results for participants differing on lyric focus, depending on whether the emotions are conveyed musically, lyrically, or both. Or, a researcher interested in explaining individual differences in musical preference might obtain a better-fitting model by including lyric focus as a factor that impacts participants' liking of different musical styles.

Given the clear utility of this construct for researchers, the goal of the current project was to create a standardized measurement of lyric focus by developing a questionnaire that is practical, reliable, and valid. In Study 1, we created the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ) by generating a large list of 121 candidate questionnaire items to measure lyric focus. We then used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on participant ratings from two independent samples to reduce these candidate items into a brief 12item measure that is easy to implement across diverse research settings.

In Study 2, we confirmed the unidimensional structure of lyric focus using confirmatory factor analysis on the 12-item LFQ. We then assessed the test-retest reliability of the LFQ by testing participants again, two weeks after the initial data collection.

In Studies 3 and 4, we aimed to establish convergent validity for the LFQ using a lyric transcription task adapted from Condit-Schultz & Huron (2015; Study 3) as well as a novel lyric comprehension task (Study 4). We predicted that participants who scored high on the LFQ should perform better on both lyric transcription and comprehension.

Finally, we present Study 5, in which we aggregated data across the first four studies. We used this larger combined sample in order to establish norms for the LFQ, as well as to explore discriminant validity by calculating correlations between lyric focus, musical training and practice, and literary activities.

Study 1: Questionnaire Creation

The objective of Study 1 was to develop a self-report scale quantifying lyric focus. Thus, a large pool of candidate items measuring multifactorial engagement with various aspects of songs were generated (see Materials below). A list of 121 candidate questionnaire items was administered to participants, and their responses were submitted to exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in order to quantify the relations between candidate items and identify a single factor associated with lyric focus. The results of this EFA were used to reduce the number of candidate items to create a targeted assessment of lyric focus, the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ).

Methods

The protocol for this study was approved by the Skidmore College Institutional Review Board.

Participants

Following guidance from Comrey & Lee (1992) and Tabachnick & Fidell (2013), we aimed to recruit at least 300 participants. 587 adult residents of the United States were recruited to participate using the Turk Prime platform (Litman et al., 2017) in two waves (n = 214 in April and n = 373 in July 2017). Participants were remunerated 75 cents for their time in April, and this was increased to $1 in July, as the length of the study was increased (see Materials below). We discarded data from participants who did not explicitly consent to participate (despite having completed the survey), did not reach the end of the survey, or indicated that they did not wish to submit their data upon finishing the survey. One additional participant's data were discarded because they provided the same response for all questionnaire items, indicating a lack of attention to the task. Following this cleaning process, data from 386 participants were submitted to analysis.

Combined across both waves of data collection, participants (170 men, 214 women, 1 non-binary) reported a mean age of 38.73 years (range = 19-98, SD = 12.99) and a mean of 14.52 years of education (range = 0 -more than 25, SD = 4.11). We collected data on musical and literary experience from 191 participants (Table 1). About half of these participants reported having formal musical training, including 18 trained vocalists. 32 of these participants were currently practicing music in some way, including 4 practicing vocalists. Approximately half of the participants reported being involved in some type of literary activity (included writing, acting, literary discourse, and/or public speaking). The data on the amount of time spent per week on literary activities included extreme values contributed by several participants. We thus created a trimmed version of these data by applying a reasonable maximum of 84 hours (12 hours per day, 7 days a week; see Table 1).

[Insert Table 1 here]

Materials

Candidate items for the LFQ. We created 121 candidate items for our lyric focus scale by considering the various ways that listeners can engage with different aspects of songs. Methods of engagement included selection (of songs to listen to), attention, emotion, memory, and production (or reproduction), and aspects of songs included lyrics, melody, harmony, rhythm, beat, vocal timbre, and instrumental timbre.

Items were constructed in the form of statements which participants could endorse on a seven-point Likert scale (Strongly disagree -Disagree -Somewhat disagree -Neither agree nor disagree -Somewhat agree -Agree -Strongly agree), and were phrased to be comprehensible to participants regardless of their level of musical training.

An example of an item targeting lyric focus is "I can remember the lyrics of a song after hearing it a couple times". An example of an item targeting a non-lyric focus is "The melody of a song can make me cry". All candidate items are available at https://osf.io/nd9q8/.

Demographics, Musical Experience, and Literary Activities.

All participants provided basic demographic information. During the second wave of data collection (July 2017), we added a section asking participants for information regarding their formal musical education, current musical practice, and current literary activities (see Participants section above), for the purpose of exploring the relation between these individual differences and scores on our Lyric Focus Questionnaire items (see Study 5).

Apparatus.

All participants accessed the study via an internet browser, and were asked to use headphones if available.

Procedure

Participants were directed via Turk Prime to a survey hosted by Qualtrics (Provo, UT). After providing informed consent, participants responded to a series of questions about their demographics, and then a series of questions about their musical and literary experience (only for second wave of data collection). Then, the 121 test items were presented with the following instructions: "The following set of questions all relate to the way in which you perceive songs (i.e., pieces which combine music with lyrics). For each item, you will respond on a scale indicating how much you agree with the statement posed, from "Strongly Disagree" to "Strongly Agree". When the question refers to lyrics, imagine lyrics in the language in which you are most proficient."

After completing the survey, participants were asked to confirm that they wished to submit their responses, and then given a code they could redeem on Turk Prime for payment. The full survey took participants an average of 13.17 minutes (SD = 7.01) to complete. The data were fully anonymized before analysis and the research team did not have access to information that could lead to personal identification, such as email or IP addresses.

Results

All analyses were carried out using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the R packages psych (version 2.4.6.26; Revelle, 2024), ez (version 4.4-0; Lawrence, 2016), and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016).

Exploratory Factor Analysis

Participant responses to the 121 candidate items were submitted to exploratory factor analysis using the principal axis method and oblimin rotation. Missing responses were interpolated with the participant's mean response to all other items (a total of 55 data points over 29 participants, with a mean of 1.90 replacements/participant, and a maximum of 8 replacements for one participant). The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy suggested that the correlational structure of the data was very suitable for a factor analysis (KMO = .91). The optimal number of factors was determined based on parallel analysis (Henson & Roberts, 2006; Matsunaga, 2010) and yielded a convergent solution of 11 factors. The 11-factor solution explained 52% of the variance with the first factor explaining 17% of the variance. The model fit was assessed according to conventional cut-off criteria from Hu and Bentler (1999) and Marsh et al. (2004), RMSEA = 0.04 (cut-off < 0.06 -0.08), Tucker-Lewis Index = 0.83 (cut-off > 0.90-0.95).

Isolating Lyric Focus

Despite the less-than-perfect model fit, given that we were most interested in isolating one of the 11 factors, we proceeded to select items with factor loadings > .60 for the first factor, and no cross-loadings with other factors (maximum absolute value loading on any other factor = .28). Inspection of these 12 items revealed that they all assessed an individual's focus on song lyrics, with some diversity in how that focus was described. For example, some items focused on emotions, others focused on attention, and yet others focused on motivation during music selection. Table 2 lists all 12 items, alongside their factor loadings, item-total correlations, and the mean and standard deviation of the participant scores.

These 12 items thus formed our Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which was submitted to further psychometric testing in Study 2. We calculated preliminary LFQ scores for participants with music and literary activities data (n = 191) by averaging their ratings across the 12 candidate items. Preliminary LFQ scores had a mean of 4.99, a median of 5.17, a standard deviation of 1.20, and an interquartile range of 1.50 (Figure 1). The distribution of the LFQ was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.72), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = 0.49), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was non-normal, W = .96, p < .001.

[Insert Table 2 here] [Insert Figure 1 here]

Other Factors

In addition to the first lyric focus factor accounting for 17% of the total variance, there were 7 further factors that included items with factor loadings > .60, and no crossloadings with other factors. The second factor included 10 items indexing a listener's focus on the instrumentation of a song (14% of total variance). The third factor included 5 items indexing a listener's focus on the singer's voice (11% of total variance). The fourth factor included 4 items indexing a listener's tendency to hum along (10% of total variance). The fifth factor included 5 items indexing a listener's ability to remember lyrics (10% of total variance). The sixth factor included 2 items indexing a listener's emotional response to melody (9% of total variance). The seventh factor included 6 items indexing a listener's focus on beat and movement (9% of total variance). The eighth factor included 1 item indexing a listener's focus on vocal harmonies (8% of total variance).

More information regarding these factors and item loadings are available on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/nd9q8/files/6jg2d).

Although the singer's voice and memory for lyrics may be related to lyric focus, we chose to pursue just the first factor in the rest of the current studies. This choice was guided by our initial motivation to investigate the relation between music and language processing. This literature (see introduction) emphasizes lab tasks assessing perception and attention to songs in real time, rather than long-term memory for specific stimuli (as indexed by memory for lyrics) or vocal timbre (as indexed by the singer's voice). Thus, we argue that the items from the first factor alone represent the best measurement of a lyric focus construct that has a meaningful impact on participants' performance in current tasks used to assess the sharing (or lack thereof) of neurocognitive resources between music and language processing.

Discussion

In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to analyze responses to a pool of 121 candidate items examining different ways participants might engage during song listening. Our results showed that 12 items loaded strongly on to a single latent factor representing lyric focus, and formed the preliminary Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ).

Intriguingly, the structure of our questionnaire items as revealed by the current EFA indicates that, contrary to our earlier hypothesis, listeners low on lyric focus are not necessarily high on focus toward a particular musical aspect. Rather, there are a number of other factors that each index the degree to which a listener is focused on various other aspects of songs. Given the many different ways that a listener could be "music focused", this result underscores the utility of targeting the lyric focus factor alone as a construct that should straightforwardly predict listeners' processing of song stimuli.

Study 2: Confirming the Structure of the LFQ

The objectives of Study 2 were to confirm the unidimensional structure of the LFQ, to establish internal consistency and test-retest reliability for the LFQ, and to confirm that Lyric Focus is statistically independent from the aspects of musical engagement usually considered by researchers. Like in Study 1, we also explored the possibility that participation in literary activities might be associated with Lyric Focus.

Thus, we administered the 12-item LFQ to a sample of participants at two time points, two weeks apart. Their responses at Time 1 were submitted to confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to confirm that the items of the LFQ load on to a single latent construct. We also calculated split-half reliability and inter-item correlations for Time 1 data to assess internal consistency. Finally, to confirm that participant responses were stable through time, we calculated the correlation between LFQ scores at Time 1 and Time 2 (i.e., test-retest reliability).

Methods

The protocol for this study was approved by the Skidmore College Institutional Review Board.

Participants

Following guidance from Comrey & Lee (1992) and Tabachnick & Fidell (1996), we aimed to recruit at least 300 participants. 364 adult residents of the United States were recruited to participate using the Turk Prime platform in August 2018. All participants who completed the study at Time 1 were invited to participate again, two weeks later (Time 2). Of the original sample, 170 participants returned to complete the study at Time 2. Participants were remunerated $1.50 for completing the first part of the study, and $2 for completing the second part of the study.

We discarded data from participants who did not explicitly consent to participate in the study (despite having completed the survey), did not reach the end of the survey, or indicated that they did not wish to submit their data upon finishing the survey.

Following this cleaning process, data from 303 participants at Time 1 and 158 returning participants at Time 2 were submitted to analysis. Participants (153 men, 149 women, 1 non-binary) reported a mean age of 34.15 years (range = 18-70, SD = 10.19) and a mean of 14.01 years of education (range = 0more than 25, SD = 4.92). We collected data on musical and literary experience from all participants (Table 3). More than half of these participants reported having formal musical training, including 36 trained vocalists. Approximately half of these participants were currently practicing music in some way, including 32 practicing vocalists.

Approximately half of participants reported being involved in some type of literary activity (included writing, acting, literary discourse, and/or public speaking). The data pertaining to the amount of time spent per week on literary activities included extreme values contributed by several participants. We thus created a trimmed version of these data by applying a reasonable maximum of 84 hours (12 hours per day, 7 days a week; see Table 3).

[Insert Table 3 here]

Materials

The 12-item LFQ (Table 2) and the demographic, musical, and literary activity questionnaires from Study 1 were used in Study 2. All participants accessed the study via an internet browser, and were asked to use headphones if available.

Procedure

At Time 1, participants were directed via Turk Prime to a survey hosted by Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, participants responded to a series of questions about their demographics, and then a series of questions about their musical and literary experience. Then, the 12 items of the LFQ were presented in a different random order for each participant with the same instructions as the previous study. After completing the survey, participants were asked to confirm that they wished to submit their responses, and then given a code they could redeem on Turk Prime for payment.

The survey at Time 1 took participants an average of 6.22 minutes (SD = 3.83) to complete.

Two weeks following the initial invitation to participate (Time 2), participants who had participated at Time 1 were invited back via Turk Prime to complete a second survey on Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, participants completed the 12 items of the LFQ (again presented in a different random order for each participant), preceded by the same instructions as were presented at Time 1. After completing the survey, participants were asked to confirm that they wished to submit their responses, and then given a code they could redeem on Turk Prime for payment. The survey at Time 2 took participants an average of 3.61 minutes (SD = 3.04) to complete.

The data were fully anonymized before analysis and the research team did not have access to information that could lead to personal identification, such as email or IP addresses.

Results

All analyses were carried out using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the R packages psych (version 2.4.6.26; Revelle, 2024), lavaan (version 0.6-18; Rosseel, 2012), ez (version 4.4-0; Lawrence, 2016), and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016).

Confirmatory Factor Analysis

Participant responses were submitted to confirmatory factor analysis, which assessed a measurement model in which all 12 items of the LFQ loaded on to a single latent variable. Missing responses were interpolated with the participant's mean response to all other items (a total of 19 data points over 18 participants, with a maximum of 2 replacements for one participant). The model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood and the variance standardization method, with factor loadings standardized by the variance of both the latent and outcome variables.

All 12 items loaded significantly on the one latent variable, with relatively high magnitude loadings (Table 4). We evaluated model fit using multiple indices, with conventional cutoff criteria from Hu & Bentler (1999) and Marsh et al. (2004) [Insert Table 4 here]

LFQ Distribution

LFQ scores at Time 1 (n = 303) had a mean of 5.28, a median of 5.50, a standard deviation of 1.25, and an interquartile range of 1.63 (Figure 2). The distribution of the LFQ was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.85), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = 0.52), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was nonnormal, W = .94, p < .001. LFQ scores at Time 2 (n = 158) had a mean of 5.14, a median of 5.33, a standard deviation of 1.22, and an interquartile range of 1.50 (Figure 2). The distribution of the LFQ was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.88), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = 0.76), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was non-normal, W = .95, p < .001.

Internal Consistency and Test-Retest Reliability

The LFQ exhibited a high degree of internal consistency. Participant LFQ scores were calculated by averaging their ratings across the 12 items. At Time 1, all possible split halves of participant scores yielded an average split half reliability of .96 (Spearman-Brown corrected; Cronbach's α = .96; Revelle's minimum split half reliability β = .95) and an average inter-item r = .70. Similarly, when participants were re-tested at Time 2, the average split-half reliability was .96 (Cronbach's α = .96; Revelle's β = .94) with an average inter-item r = .70. LFQ scores were very stable over time. The correlation between participant scores at Time 1 and Time 2 was r(156) = .88, p < .001. There was no significant difference between participants' LFQ scores at Time 1 and Time 2 (M T1-T2 = 0.03, SD T1- T2 = 0.61), t(157) = 0.60, p = .55, d = 0.05.

[Insert Figure 2 here]

Discussion

In the current study, we used confirmatory factor analysis to show that our 12 candidate LFQ items all loaded on to a single latent factor. This LFQ questionnaire was completed by participants in less than four minutes, making it a highly practical tool for research use. LFQ scores in our sample tended to be high (> 5 on a 7-point scale), and were distributed with a leftward skew, confirming our preliminary exploration from Study 1. Further analyses confirmed that the LFQ showed strong internal consistency, and that LFQ scores are very stable over time.

Study 3: Lyric Recall

The objective of Study 3 was to show construct validity for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire by demonstrating that LFQ scores are correlated with a relevant task:

Participants' ability to recall novel song lyrics immediately after hearing them. To that end, we used an existing Lyric Recall task developed by Condit-Schultz and Huron (2015), in which participants were presented with short song excerpts in varying styles and were asked to report the lyrics immediately following exposure.

It is important to note that the LFQ does not index general memory for lyrics (see Study 1). However, the lyric memory items that we discarded in Study 1 describe familiar songs, or memory over multiple listenings. The current task was chosen because cognitive neuroscience research on music-language sharing tends to use novel, rather than familiar songs as stimuli. And, given our interest in perceptualattentional processing, we wanted to validate the LFQ with a task that required immediate response, maximizing the effect of individual differences in lyric focus on recall.

Our initial sample was collected online, and we followed up with a second sample collected in the lab in order to gain more control of testing conditions. We predicted that participants reporting higher LFQ scores would perform better on this Lyric Recall task.

Methods

The protocol for this study was approved by the Skidmore College Institutional Review Board.

Participants

Recent studies of individual differences within music cognition (i.e., with the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ); Mas-Herrero et al., 2012) have observed correlations between the BMRQ and behaviour between r = .20 -.30 (Ferreri & Rodriguez-Fornells, 2017). Guided by these data, we assumed a true correlation of r = .25 between the LFQ and lyric recall performance, which can be detected by a onetailed test (assuming a positive correlation) with power = .80 and a sample of n = 95.

Thus, we aimed to recruit at least 100 participants.

Online sample. The first sample was collected online in December 2017-January 2018.97 adult residents of the United States were recruited to participate through the Skidmore College introductory psychology participation pool as well as the Turk Prime platform. Skidmore participants were remunerated 1 research credit and Turk Prime participants were remunerated $4.00 for completing the study. We discarded data from participants who did not explicitly consent to participate in the study (despite having completed the survey), did not reach the end of the survey, or indicated that they did not wish to submit their data upon finishing the survey. Following this cleaning process, data from 67 participants were submitted to analysis. Participants (26 men, 40 women, 1 did not specify gender) reported a mean age of 26.42 years (range = 18-64, SD = 11.89) and a mean of 12.52 years of education (range = 0-19, SD = 4.64). We collected data on musical and literary experience from all participants (Table 5). About half of these participants reported having formal musical training, including 9 trained vocalists. Less than half of these participants were currently practicing music in some way, including 7 practicing vocalists. Less than half of participants reported being involved in some type of literary activity (included writing, acting, literary discourse, and/or public speaking).

Lab sample.

The second sample was collected in the laboratory in January through April 2023.64 students at Skidmore College were recruited to participate using the introductory psychology participation pool. Participants were remunerated 1 research credit for completing the study. We discarded data from participants who did not explicitly consent to participate in the study (despite having completed the survey), did not reach the end of the survey, or indicated that they did not wish to submit their data upon finishing the survey. Following this cleaning process, data from 53 participants were submitted to analysis. Participants (14 men, 36 women, 3 non-binary) reported a mean age of 18.88 years (range = 18-22, SD = 0.92) and a mean of 12.79 years of education (range = 1-19, SD = 3.56). We collected data on musical and literary experience from all participants (Table 5). Almost three-quarters of participants reported having formal musical training, including 18 trained vocalists. Approximately one-third of these participants were currently practicing music in some way, including 8 practicing vocalists. More than half of participants reported being involved in some type of literary activity (included writing, acting, literary discourse, and/or public speaking).

[Insert Table 5 here]

Materials

Questionnaires. The 12-item LFQ (Table 2) and the demographic, musical, and literary activity questionnaires from Studies 1 and 2 were used in Study 3.

Lyric Recall Task.

The validation task was adapted from Condit-Schultz & Huron's (2015) experiment, which explored lyric intelligibility across multiple genres. We obtained the stimuli from Experiment 2 of Condit-Schultz & Huron (2015), as well as the validated answer key developed by those authors for scoring these items. These stimuli were comprised of 40 brief clips of relatively unfamiliar songs with lyrics in English, traversing 12 genres: Avant-garde, Blues, Classical, Country, Folk, Jazz, Pop/Rock, Rhythm and Blues, Rap, Reggae, Religious, and Stage & Screen/Theater. The task was designed to challenge listeners, as one quarter of the items were drawn from a stimulus pool evoking average (70%-80%) performance, and three quarters were drawn from a stimulus pool evoking poor performance (<70%; see Condit-Schultz & Huron, 2015 for details). On average, the lyrics from these clips were 7.43 words long (SD = 1.84).

Apparatus.

All participants accessed the study via an internet browser, with the experiment hosted by Qualtrics. Online participants were asked to use headphones if available. Lab participants were all tested on PCs running the Ubuntu operating system, Firefox internet browser, and listened to the experiment with Sennheiser closed-back headphones.

Procedure

Online participants were directed to Qualtrics via Turk Prime or Sona (the software used by Skidmore's introductory psychology pool), and lab participants were tested on computers with the Qualtrics survey open in a browser.

After providing informed consent, participants used an example sound to set a comfortable volume on their speakers or headphones. Then they responded to a series of questions about their demographics, followed by a series of questions about their musical and literary experience. Next, they were presented with the Lyric Recall task via the following instructions: "You will hear a number of short (3-23 seconds) musical excerpts from a wide variety of songs. For each excerpt you should listen carefully, and then report back the lyrics as best you can. Each music excerpt will load and play automatically. Then, you will be asked to type the lyrics you heard. You'll only get one chance to hear each excerpt, but you can take as much time as you like to write down the lyrics. For each excerpt you will be asked to indicate via check box anytime you recognize, the song, the singer, or both."

Participants were then presented with the 40 trials in random order. On each trial, participants clicked a button to indicate they were ready for each trial to begin, and then were presented with one of the 40 clips. When the clip finished, the survey automatically advanced to the next page, which asked the participant to type out the lyrics they had just heard. Finally, the participant was asked whether they recognized the artist or song.

After participants completed the Lyric Recall task, the 12 items of the LFQ were presented in a different random order for each participant, with the same instructions as for the previous studies.

After completing the survey, participants were asked to confirm that they wished to submit their responses, and Turk Prime participants were given a code they could redeem for payment. The survey took Turk Prime participants an average of 30.57 minutes (SD = 10.61) to complete. Online student participants took an average of 31.18 minutes (SD = 15.51; 2 outliers took over 24 hours) to complete the study. Lab participants took an average of 31.95 minutes (SD = 9.33) to complete the study.

The data were fully anonymized before analysis and the research team did not have access to information that could lead to personal identification, such as email or IP addresses.

Lyric Recall Task Coding

Participant responses in the Lyric Recall Task were coded for accuracy using the answer key developed by Condit-Schultz & Huron (2015). In addition to listing the correct lyrics for each of the 40 audio clips, the answer key also provided rules about how to score intelligible misspellings, homophones, and other transcription errors. Due to the nature of the transcription errors in our data, we added additional coding rules for some of the questions. Both Condit-Schultz & Huron's original answer key and our adapted version can be found at https://osf.io/nd9q8/.

For each trial, participants were assigned a point for every word that was recalled correctly, and no points for each word that was incorrectly recalled or skipped.

Responses were considered invalid and discarded if the participant reported recognizing the artist or song. Across both samples, participants rarely reported recognizing the artist or song (M = 1.25 trials/40, SD = 1.85, range = 0-10). Task performance was calculated for each participant as a proportion of words reported correctly from the lyrics of valid trials (i.e., trials for which they did not recognize the artist or song).

Results

All analyses were carried out using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the R packages psych (version 2.4.6.26; Revelle, 2024), ez (version 4.4-0; Lawrence, 2016), and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016).

An analysis plan was pre-registered after data collection but in advance of data access and analysis (https://osf.io/g35ym).

LFQ Distribution

As in Studies 1 and 2, missing responses on the LFQ were interpolated with the participant's mean LFQ score (a total of 3 data points over 3 participants). LFQ scores in Study 3 were similar to previous studies. Online LFQ scores had a mean of 5.04, a median of 5.08, a standard deviation of 1.02, and an interquartile range of 1.33. The distribution of the online LFQ scores was skewed to the left (skewness = -1.13), was leptokurtic (excess kurtosis = 2.48), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was non-normal, W = .93, p = .001. Lab LFQ scores had a mean of 4.93, a median of 5.17, a standard deviation of 1.07, and an interquartile range of 2.00. The distribution of the lab LFQ scores was also skewed to the left (skewness = -0.34), was modestly platykurtic (excess kurtosis = -0.95), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was non-normal, W = .95, p = .02. LFQ scores did not differ significantly between the online sample and lab sample (M = 4.93, SD = 1.07), t(118) = 0.57, p = .57, d = 0.01. Distributions for the samples can be seen in Figure 3.

[insert Figure 3 here]

Lyric Recall Task

Participant scores reflected the proportion of words reported correctly from the lyrics of valid trials (i.e., trials for which they did not recognize the artist or song). Online Lyric Recall scores had a mean of .42, a median of .43, a standard deviation of .10, and an interquartile range of .14. The distribution of the online Lyric Recall scores was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.53), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = -0.19) and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was normal, W = .97, p = .07. Lab Lyric Recall scores had a mean of .47, a median of .49, a standard deviation of ..09, and an interquartile range of .11. The distribution of the lab Lyric Recall scores was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.54), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = -0.64), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was non-normal, W = .95, p = .04. Lyric Recall scores were lower for the online sample than the lab sample, t(118) = 2.98, p = .003, d = .06. The relatively low performance in both groups is consistent with Condit-Schultz and Huron's (2015) Experiment 2 average score of 47% and indicates that, as expected, the task was challenging for participants (Figure 4).

[insert Figure 4 here]

LFQ and Lyric Recall

Finally, to assess construct validity for the LFQ, we correlated performance on the Lyric Recall task with the LFQ. There was no significant correlation between participants' Lyric Recall scores and the LFQ for the combined sample (online and lab together), r(118) = .07, p = .44.

Discussion

In the current study, we attempted to demonstrate construct validity for the LFQ by having participants perform a Lyric Recall task, with the prediction that participants who scored higher on the LFQ would be better at identifying lyrics in unfamiliar songs. This prediction was not confirmed in either of the two samples. However, data from this study did converge with estimates of central tendency (~5) and variability (~1) for LFQ scores from the previous studies.

Interestingly, we noticed that some participants provided lyrics that were narratively coherent with the original song, even when the words were incorrect. This informed our second attempt at establishing construct validity for the LFQ, this time with a task that measured listeners' narrative comprehension of lyrics.

Study 4: Lyric Comprehension

The objective of Study 4 was to show construct validity for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire by demonstrating that LFQ scores are correlated with a new task measuring participants' narrative comprehension of lyrics. Study 3 indicated that lyric focus, as measured by the LFQ, does not predict performance on a task requiring precise reporting of the exact lyrics from song excerpts. However, we did observe that participant responses in the Lyric Recall task varied in terms of how well they matched the general meaning of the lyrics, even if they failed to report the exact lyrics correctly.

Accordingly, it is possible that lyric focus is associated with processing of the semantic content of the lyrics (Lyric Comprehension) rather than processing of the lexical content (Lyric Recall).

To that end, we developed a novel Lyric Comprehension task, in which participants were presented with short song excerpts and then were asked to answer comprehension questions about the lyrics immediately following exposure. We predicted that participants reporting higher LFQ scores would perform better on this Lyric Comprehension task.

Methods

The protocol for this study was approved by the Skidmore College Institutional Review Board.

Participants

Following the sample estimation logic used in Study 3, we aimed to recruit at least 100 participants. 114 participants were recruited through the Skidmore College introductory psychology participation pool in Fall 2023, and were remunerated 1 research credit for completing the study. We discarded data from three participants due to technical difficulties and one participant who reported having an auditory processing delay. Thus, data from 111 participants were submitted to analysis. Participants (35 men, 71 women, 5 non-binary) reported a mean age of 18.08 years (SD = 1.03) and a mean of 13.33 years of education (range = 1-19, SD = 2.80).

We collected data on musical and literary experience from all participants (Table 6).

Over 80 participants reported having formal musical training, including 28 trained vocalists. About a fifth of participants were currently practicing music in some way, including 9 practicing vocalists. Less than half of participants reported being involved in some type of literary activity (included writing, acting, literary discourse, and/or public speaking).

[Insert Table 6 here]

Materials

Questionnaires. The 12-item LFQ (Table 2) and the demographic, musical, and literary activity questionnaires from Studies 1, 2, and 3 were used in Study 4.

Stimuli.

A total of 34 popular songs by Australian artists were used as sources of audio clips for this study. We selected songs from Australia because they are sung in English, from familiar popular genres, but were likely to be unfamiliar to our participants.

Lyric Focus likely impacts participants' experiences with both familiar and unfamiliar songs, and participants are likely considering both familiar and unfamiliar songs when responding to LFQ items. However, we chose to employ unfamiliar stimuli in the current experiment in order to control for the impact of differential exposure to specific songs on our participants' memory for lyrics.

Initially, a total of 50 songs were considered for use as stimuli, but some were eliminated due to possible familiarity or a lack of narrative content. Specific sections of the remaining songs were selected based on their lyrical content. Selected lyrics contained narrative content that told a story or described a scene. All of the finalized audio clips were edited using the program Audacity and exported as audio files (.wav).

On average, the clips were 21.44 seconds long (SD = 4.39). Similar to the clips from Condit-Schultz & Huron (2015), all of the clips used in this study were completed musical phrases and lyrical thoughts. Information about artists, song titles, genre, and clip length are provided at https://osf.io/r92q4.

Lyric Comprehension (LC) Questions.

Three LC questions were designed for each of the thirty-four clips based on the guidelines for creating comprehension questions from Day & Park (2005). Questions were therefore written in multiple choice, True/False, Yes/No, and Who/What/Where/Why/How Questions. For example, one of the clips contains the lyric "The TV's on that's what it's for" and the corresponding LC question was ""Is the TV on in the background?", with the correct answer being "Yes".

All LC questions are posted at https://osf.io/r92q4.

Distractor Questions.

In addition to the three LC questions, three distractor questions were also designed so that participants would be less likely to catch on that the study was only measuring their lyric comprehension. These questions were related to the clip's musical content. Distractors included questions like "What instruments did you hear?" or "During the clip, did you find yourself moving to the beat?" All distractor questions are posted at https://osf.io/r92q4.

Apparatus.

Participants accessed the study via an internet browser, with the experiment hosted by Qualtrics (Provo, UT). The study was run on PCs running the Ubuntu operating system, Firefox internet browser, and sounds were presented with Sennheiser closed-back headphones.

Procedure

The experiment took place in the Skidmore Music and Cognition lab. First, participants read the study description and provided informed consent. Following this, the research assistant provided headphones to the participant and instructed them: "Throughout the study you will hear clips of various songs across genres. Listen carefully to each song. You will be asked to answer questions about what you hear. At the halfway point there will be a two-minute break. Please exit the room and I will tell you when the two minutes is up. Lastly, for each of the questions try your best to put an answer down for something even if you are unsure. Any answer is better than leaving something blank. Let me know if you have any questions throughout the study."

Participants used an example sound to set a comfortable volume on the headphones, and then completed the questionnaires on demographics, musical experience, and literary activities. Before beginning the lyric comprehension task, the participants reread the task instructions, which reminded them to listen to each excerpt carefully and that audio clips would be played automatically.

The 34 experimental trials were presented to participants in a randomized order.

Participants clicked a button to indicate they were ready for each trial to begin, and then were presented with one of the 34 audio clips. When the audio clip finished, the survey automatically advanced to the next page, which presented six questions (three lyric comprehension questions, three distractor questions) in randomized order. After answering the six questions, the participant was asked whether they recognized the artist or song. If they answered yes to either of these questions, they were asked to specify the name of the artist and/or song by typing it into a response box.

Halfway through the trials (i.e., after 17 trials), participants were asked to exit the room and take a two-minute break before returning to complete the 17 remaining experimental trials. After participants completed the lyric comprehension task, the 12 items of the LFQ were presented in a different random order for each participant, with the same instructions as for the previous studies. Finally, participants were asked to confirm that they wished to submit their responses. As part of the debriefing process, researchers asked participants to provide feedback on their experience with the experiment, if they wished. Participants took an average of 59.18 minutes (SD = 20.06) to complete the study.

The data were fully anonymized before analysis and the research team did not have access to information that could lead to personal identification, such as email or IP addresses.

Lyric Comprehension Task Coding

All coding materials are posted at https://osf.io/z9myv. The second author and two additional coders scored the data from this study. Data were assigned such that two coders scored each participant's responses. An answer key was developed by the second author with all the correct answers for each LC question (all LC questions are posted at https://osf.io/r92q4). There were 102 LC questions in total; however, errors in two LC questions were found, and therefore removed from the analysis. As a result, coders scored 100 LC questions, such that participants could score a maximum of 100 lyric comprehension points.

Coders assigned a point for every question that was answered correctly, and no points for each question that was incorrectly answered or skipped. Responses were considered invalid and discarded if the participant correctly recognized the artist or song. Only three participants recognized songs or artists presented in the study: One participant identified the artist of audio clip 26 (Drapht), another participant identified the song title of audio clip 18 ("What About Me"), and the third participant identified the artist of audio clip 36 (Hillside Worship).

After all responses were coded, intercoder agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa. Agreement was extremely high, with Cohen's kappa between the three coder pairs for the LC questions ranging from 0.988 -0.998. For the few disagreements that arose, the second author finalized the scoring. Then, task performance was calculated for each participant as a percentage of lyric comprehension questions answered correctly for valid trials (i.e., trials for which they did not recognize the artist or song). Distractor questions were not scored due to our focus on lyric processing and because they were often designed with no clear correct answer.

Results

All analyses were carried out using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the R packages psych (version 2.4.6.26; Revelle, 2024), ez (version 4.4-0; Lawrence, 2016), and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016).

LFQ Distribution

As in Studies 1, 2, and 3, missing responses on the LFQ were interpolated with the participant's mean LFQ score (a total of 1 data point for 1 participant). LFQ scores had a mean of 4.41, a median of 4.58, a standard deviation of 1.18, and an interquartile range of 1.67 (Figure 5). The distribution of the LFQ scores was skewed to the left (skewness = -0.41), was mesokurtic (excess kurtosis = -0.13), and the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality indicated that the distribution was normal, W = .98, p = .14.

[Insert Figure 5 here]

Lyric Comprehension Task

Task performance on the Lyric Comprehension task was calculated as a proportion of correct responses on valid trials (i.e., trials for which they did not recognize the artist or song). Lyric Comprehension scores had a mean of .64, a median of .64, a standard deviation of .09, and an interquartile range of .11. Scores were negatively skewed (skewness = -0.62) and modestly leptokurtic (excess kurtosis = 1.24). The Shapiro-Wilk test indicates that the distribution is non-normal, W = .97, p = .02.

Participant scores indicated that this task was somewhat less challenging for participants than the Lyric Recall task from Study 3. The distribution of Lyric Comprehension scores can be seen in Figure 6.

[Insert Figure 6 here]

LFQ and Lyric Comprehension

To assess construct validity for the LFQ, we correlated performance on the Lyric Comprehension task with the LFQ (Figure 7). There was a significant positive correlation between participants' lyric comprehension and their LFQ scores, r(109) = .23, p = .01 (r s (109) = .17, p = .08).

[Insert Figure 7 here]

Self-Identification and LFQ

Incidentally, three participants identified themselves as non-lyric listeners in free response items or directly to the research assistant. These participants had LFQ scores that closely matched their self-assessment (z = -2.31, -2.03, and -2.74 within the Study 4 sample, respectively). Interestingly, their lyric comprehension scores varied from average to low (z = 0.01, -0.93, and -3.86 within the Study 4 sample, respectively).

Discussion

Although LFQ scores in this study were slightly lower than previous estimates of central tendency in our previous studies, the distribution of these scores were similar to our previous samples. The main goal of the current study was to demonstrate construct validity for the LFQ with a lyric comprehension task, with the prediction that participants who scored higher on the LFQ would be better at comprehending lyrics in unfamiliar songs. We demonstrated a positive correlation between LFQ and lyric comprehension scores, indicating that the LFQ measures an aspect of song processing that was reflected in participant behaviour in a relevant task.

Study 5: Aggregating Data Across Studies

In this final study, we analyzed aggregated data across the four previous studies. This aggregated sample included measures of the LFQ as well as musical and literary activities for 725 independent participants. The analysis of this larger sample was designed to (1) create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and (2) enable exploratory analysis of discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. Although this aggregate analysis can provide interesting insights that will deepen our initial understanding of the Lyric Focus construct, the results should be interpreted with caution, given the lack of uniformity in testing conditions between the studies.

Results

All analyses were carried out using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the R packages psych (version 2.4.6.26; Revelle, 2024), ez (version 4.4-0; Lawrence, 2016), and ggplot2 (version 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016).

Initial Norms for the LFQ

The distribution of the LFQ was quite stable from study to study. The LFQ scores when the four studies were combined (n = 725) had a mean of 5.02, a median of 5.17, a standard deviation of 1.23, and an interquartile range of 1.58. Scores were spread across the 1-7 range, with a negatively skewed mesokurtic distribution (skewness = -0.67, excess kurtosis = 0.29). The Shapiro-Wilk test indicates that the distribution is non-normal, W = .97, p < .001. This non-normality can be partly attributed to restricted range at the top of the distribution (Figure 8).

LFQ scores varied depending on participants' reported gender (nmen = 314, Mmen = 4.74, SDmen = 1.35; n non-binary = 10, Mnon-binary = 5.63, SDnon-binary = 0.91; nwomen = 400, Mwomen = 5.23, SDwomen = 1.09), F(2, 721) = 15.33, p < .001, GES = .04. Follow-up comparisons conducted with Tukey's HSD indicated that this was due to the LFQ scores for women being significantly higher than those for men (Figure 9).

Our participants varied in age from 17 to 74 years (M = 30.86, SD = 12.07). This distribution was positively skewed (skewness = 1.06), with a median of 29. LFQ scores were not significantly associated with age, r(719) =.05, p = .14.

[Insert Figures 8 and 9 here]

LFQ, Musical Experience, and Literary Activities

All continuous self-report measures of musical and literary engagement were treated for outliers using winsorization (95 th percentile) prior to analysis using parametric statistics (i.e., t tests and Pearson's r). Because the LFQ has a left-skewed distribution, we report below both the traditional parametric tests as well as appropriate nonparametric counterparts.

Trained Musicianship. Combined across studies, there was no difference in LFQ scores between trained musicians (n trainY = 425, M trainY = 5.05, SD trainY = 1.23) and participants who had not received musical training (n trainN = 299, M trainN = 4.98, SD trainN = 1.23), t(722) = 0.82, p = .41, d = 0.003.

Duration of Musical Training.

In the combined sample, LFQ scores were modestly negatively correlated with duration of training for musicians, r(420) = -.16, p < .001. (Figure 10).

[Insert Figure 10 here] Age of Onset of Musical Training In the combined sample, LFQ scores were modestly positively correlated with age of onset of training for musicians, r(417) = .13, p = .001. (Figure 11).

[Insert Figure 11 here] Type of Musical Training. In the combined sample, there was no difference in LFQ scores based on the type of musical training (vocal vs. instrumental vs. no training) (n trainVox = 109, M trainVox = 5.13, SD trainVox = 1.25; n trainInstr = 316, M trainInstr = 5.03, SD trainInstr = 1.23; n trainN = 299, M trainN = 4.98, SD trainN = 1.23), F(2, 721) = 0.60, p = .55, GES = .002.

Current Musical Practice.

In the combined sample, practicing musicians did not differ from participants who are not practicing music on the LFQ (n pracY = 238, M pracY = 5.13, SD pracY = 1.34; n pracN = 487, M pracN = 4.97, SD pracN = 1.17), t(723) = 1.71, p = .09, d = .008.

Amount and Type of Musical Practice.

In the combined sample, weekly hours of practice was not correlated with the LFQ, r(232) = -.01, p = .93. There were differences in LFQ scores based on the type of musical practice (vocal vs. instrumental vs. not practicing; n pracVox = 45, M pracVox = 5.49, SD pracVox = 1.20; n pracInstr = 162, M pracInstr = 5.05, SD pracInstr = 1.40; n pracN = 487, M pracN = 4.97, SD pracN = 1.17), F(2, 691) = 3.80, p = .02, GES = .01 (Figure 12). Follow-up comparisons using Tukey's HSD indicated that this effect was driven by practicing vocalists having significantly higher LFQ scores than people who were not currently practicing music, p = .02.

[Insert Figure 12 here] Literary Activities. In the combined sample, LFQ scores for participants who reported being engaged in literary activities (n litY = 348, M litY = 5.17, SD litY = 1.21) were significantly higher than LFQ scores for those who did not (n litY = 377, M litN = 4.89, SD litN = 1.23), t(723) = 3.03, p = .003, d = 0.01. Like in previous studies, we trimmed the data for weekly hours of literary activities, considering data from participants who reported a realistic maximum of 84 hours per week. Weekly hours of literary activities was not correlated with the LFQ, r(345) = .08, p = .16.

Discussion

Overall, the distribution for the LFQ was quite similar across studies, and accordingly their aggregate distribution converged with previous observations of a mean LFQ score of approximately 5 out of 7, a standard deviation close to 1, and a negatively skew. Inconsistent associations between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities in this aggregate sample indicated that Lyric Focus is at least in part independent from engagement with music and literary activities. In cases where there were significant associations between these constructs, the size of the effect was small, and was sometimes unstable, such that applying different statistical assumptions (i.e., normality, Winsorization for outliers) impacted the statistical significance of the effect. Future research will need to be conducted to clarify the existence and extent of the exact relation between these variables under more controlled conditions, and with samples that are diverse in terms of musical culture, age, geography, language, and more.

General Discussion

The goal of the current project was to develop the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), a survey tool that researchers can use to measure lyric focus. Our aim was for this assessment to exhibit three properties: (1) Practicality, (2) validity, and (3) reliability.

In terms of practicality, the final questionnaire consisted of 12 items (reduced from the original pool of 121 candidate items) which can be administered in less than 5 minutes as part of a larger study. In terms of validity, we refined the construct lyric focus construct through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and high inter-item correlations that provided evidence that the lyric focus construct is unidimensional in structure. We demonstrated convergent validity by showing that LFQ scores are significantly correlated with performance on a lyric comprehension task (but not a task requiring exact lyric transcription). We demonstrated discriminant validity by showing that lyric focus is distinct from musicianship and engagement with literary activity. In terms of reliability, we showed strong consistency in participant responses on the LFQ collected two weeks apart.

We believe that the LFQ will be of high utility to researchers conducting research with song stimuli, and particularly to those who are interested in questions regarding the relation between language and music processing. Future research should be aimed at refining the LFQ, expanding its use, and increasing our understanding of the lyric focus construct.

Refining the LFQ

The current version of the LFQ is psychometrically robust and practical to use.

Yet, our data indicate possible avenues by which we might be able to reduce the LFQ items further. Specifically, our internal consistency measurements (Study 2) were quite high, indicating a notable degree of shared variance between the items of the LFQ. We chose to maintain the 12 items in the current LFQ because they measure cognitively distinct aspects of lyric focus (i.e., emotion, attention, motivation, semantics, memory). These distinct aspects make the LFQ applicable to a wide audience of researchers and importantly, they provide the grounds for theory-driven investigations of lyric focus (see below, in the section on Exploring Lyric Focus).

That said, intriguing work by Konrath et al. (2014) suggests that a construct as complex as narcissism can be effectively measured for certain contexts with a single item. In the context of the LFQ, Condit-Schultz & Huron (2015) asked their participants to report how attentive they are to lyrics and how important lyrics are to them when they normally listen to music. They found that performance on their lyric intelligibility task (which was adapted for our first attempt at validation of the LFQ in Study 3) was marginally predicted by participant responses on the single "importance" item. Future work could explore the viability of creating a "micro-LFQ" ( similar One idiosyncracy of the LFQ is the shape of the distribution. As shown in our aggregated data (Study 5), participant LFQ scores are distributed with a negative skew, such that scores are clustered toward the top of the range. This does not appear to be a ceiling effect, as the frequency of scores decreases past the peak of the distribution (~5/7). Yet, it does potentially restrict the variability captured on the higher end of the lyric focus scale, which could attenuate correlations calculated between LFQ scores and other measures. Issues associated with this potential restricted range will need to be considered as we expand the use of the LFQ in more and different types of participants (see next section).

A second idiosyncrasy to note is that in the current studies we presented LFQ items to participants in randomized order, which is atypical for questionnaires. Given the high internal consistency and single-factor structure of the LFQ, we argue that it is unlikely that order of presentation will have impacts on LFQ scores. Thus, we recommend for simplicity that future use of the instrument (see next section) presents items to participants in the order listed in Table 2.

Expanding the Use of the LFQ

As with any novel measurement, an initial goal will be to establish norms for diverse populations for the LFQ beyond the initial combined sample in this study of n = 725, especially through collaboration with other research groups. Of particular interest will be to expand the use of the LFQ outside of the typical WEIRD (Henrich et al., 2010) young adult sample. Versions of the LFQ are currently being deployed in projects focused on sensorimotor processing, mapping anatomy across the brain to multifactorial behavioural measurements in healthy and clinical samples across the lifespan, and exploring musical preference in francophone cochlear implant users. Establishing norms for the LFQ across samples and in different languages will make this measure available to more researchers and help both to refine the tool itself (see above) as well as sharpen our understanding of the lyric focus construct (see below). These efforts will be reported as they develop on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/nd9q8/).

Exploring Lyric Focus

This is the first foray, to our knowledge, into gaining a standardized empirical understanding of the construct we are calling lyric focus. We understand lyric focus to be intuitively accessible: Asking a group of lay persons whether they are "lyric listeners"

or "music listeners" tends to produce responses with low latency and high confidence.

We also understand lyric focus to be multi-faceted: The LFQ items measure listeners report of their experience with lyrics as it relates to emotion, attention, motivation, semantics, and memory. Future studies of the LFQ will be aimed at bettering our understanding of these different facets, including explorations of attention and memory, as well as the role of musical experience in lyric processing.

Future research should seek to better understand the cognitive foundations of lyric focus. Is this individual difference primarily driven by a particular cognitive process (e.g., attention) that has a reportable impact on the others (e.g., memory, emotion, semantics), or is it a heterogenous construct such that two listeners who are both high in lyric focus can arrive there by different means (i.e., one person's attention is highly oriented towards lyrics, whereas the second person has a very strong verbal memory)?

In addition to clarifying the lyric focus construct, experiments along these lines will provide additional convergent and discriminant validation data for the LFQ by revealing how the LFQ (specific items as well as the overall score) indexes (or does not index) these different aspects of lyric processing.

In order to advance discriminant validity for the LFQ, additional work should further explore the relation between musical experience and lyric focus. It would have been straightforward to hypothesize that singers might be higher in lyric focus than instrumentalists, or that level of musical engagement (through either training or practice) might be associated with lyric focus. In contrast, our data over four studies indicate no systematic relation of lyric focus with musical experience, nor with engagement in literary activities. That said, it is possible that specific aspects of musical experience or lyric processing that have not been well-captured in the current study are meaningfully associated. Future work will benefit by expanding the measurement of musical experience through existing tools (e.g., musical ability as assessed by the Gold-MSI, Müllensiefen et al., 2014 or PROMS, Law & Zentner, 2012) in combination with better understanding of lyric focus, as discussed above.
